description.value: The study investigated whether perceptual guesses and free decisions share neural representations by using fMRI searchlight pattern classification to cross-predict choices between the two decision types.

design.value: An event-related fMRI study in which participants made category choices about pianos and chairs using three different conditions: high-visibility perceptual choices, zero-visibility perceptual guesses, and free choices.

description.value: A questionnaire used to assess adherence to the task instructions and the success of the experimental manipulation, including whether participants noticed the missing object images and when they made their free decisions.
Interviews used to assess whether participants noticed the missing object images and to determine when they made their free decisions.

source_definition.value: Trials were assigned to piano- and chair-trials according to participants' choices.
The experiment implemented three conditions: high visibility, perceptual guessing, and free decision.
Separate regressors were used for piano and chair trials, individually for each experimental condition and each run; the univariate control analyses modelled the stimuli.

Additional control decoding analyses examined motor responses across all conditions; participants used the right index- and middle finger, with response mappings pseudo-randomized on either side of the fixation cross.
The absolute difference in percentage of decisions, averaged across PGC and FDC: BI = (| pianos (%) − chairs (%) |).
Participants were divided into two groups with respect to their decision balance by median split: BI high and BI low.

description.value: Sixteen right-handed participants with normal or corrected to normal visual acuity gave written informed consent and participated in the study. One participant indicated that he had noticed the missing object images and was excluded. The data from the remaining 15 participants (7 female; mean age 25 years; range 21–28) were used for the analyses.

task_description.value: Participants made category choices about pianos and chairs using three different conditions. In the high visibility condition, a clearly visible piano or chair was presented and participants identified its category. In the perceptual guessing condition, only a strongly masked neutral noise image was presented and participants believed they were making difficult perceptual guesses. In the free decision condition, the same stimulus sequence was presented but participants spontaneously and freely chose either piano or chair, whatever category first came to mind, while ignoring the visual display.

instructions.value: For the high visibility and perceptual guessing conditions, participants categorized the presented or believed-to-be-presented object as piano or chair. For the free decision condition, participants were instructed to spontaneously choose the category that first came to mind, independent of the presentation, to choose an object category rather than a response button, not to change their mind after making a decision, and always to make a decision even if uncertain.

stimuli.value: Twenty-four pictures of pianos and chairs were transformed into greyscale 400 × 400 pixel images and presented on a grey background. Two scrambled masks were used as pre- and post-masks. The invisibility condition used one noise image consisting of scrambled phase textures.

instrument.value: Siemens TRIO 3 T scanner (Erlangen, Germany) with a standard head coil

description.value: Functional MRI volumes of the whole brain were acquired using 42 axial slices with a 1 mm gap. Within each of six runs, 208 volumes were acquired for each participant using gradient-echo EPI. The first two volumes of every scan were discarded by default to allow for magnetic saturation effects.

description.value: Motion-corrected and unsmoothed brain images were used for the GLM and subsequent searchlight decoding analyses. Decoding accuracy maps were normalized to standard stereotaxic space using the Montreal Neurological Institute EPI template and smoothed with a 6 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel.

description.value: For conventional univariate analyses, all data were motion corrected to the first volume of the first run, normalized to MNI space, resampled to a voxel size of 3 × 3 × 3 mm, and smoothed with an 8 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel.

model_settings.value: For each run, trials were modelled as events beginning with presentation of the cue. Piano and chair trials were modelled in separate regressors for each condition and run. The model captured both the cue and object periods.

A searchlight cluster was defined as a sphere with a radius of 4 voxels around each central voxel. GLM parameter estimates were extracted for each searchlight voxel, category, run, participant, and condition. The classifier used a fixed regularisation parameter C = 1 and six-fold cross-validation, training on all but one run and testing on the remaining independent run.
Normalized and smoothed three-dimensional maps of local decoding accuracy values were analysed voxel by voxel across all participants.

model_type.value: cross-condition classification with ANOVA and inclusive conjunction test

model_settings.value: Pattern vectors from one condition were used to train the classifier and predict decisions in the other condition. Both directions of cross-condition classification were performed, followed by an ANOVA and an inclusive conjunction test; only regions supporting both directions were considered significant.

estimator.value: ANOVA followed by an inclusive conjunction test

model_settings.value: Independent-samples two-tailed T-tests compared decoding accuracies between groups divided by median split on the balance indicator, for whole-brain average searchlight results and specific searchlight clusters.

description.value: On each trial, the sequence contained a clearly visible object image, either a piano or a chair. Participants were asked to identify the category of the presented object.

name.value: perceptual guessing condition (PGC), also called low visibility condition

description.value: Participants were given the same categorization task but the timing of the stimuli was chosen to yield strong masking and the sequence only contained a neutral noise image instead of an object. The condition was in fact a zero-visibility condition, although participants believed they were making difficult perceptual guesses.

The presentation was identical to the low visibility condition, with no differential visual information. Participants were asked to spontaneously and freely choose either piano or chair, whatever category came first to their minds, while ignoring the visual stimulus display.
